title: System, Processes & macOS Tools
sub: See what your Mac is running, stop it safely, and query hardware, disks, logs and settings from the shell
goals: Explain what a process is and read ps, top and lsof output
Stop, pause and restart processes with signals, and manage background jobs in zsh
Inspect services with launchctl and packages with brew
Query hardware, OS, memory, disks and power with sysctl, system_profiler, diskutil, vm_stat and pmset
Read and write settings with defaults and read logs with log show
Combine these tools into a one-screen sysinfo.zsh report

blocks.text: Every program you run becomes a **process**, and macOS lets you list, measure, pause and stop all of them from the shell. This chapter covers processes and jobs first, then the macOS-specific command-line tools that report on your hardware, disks, services, logs and settings. Many of them are read-only and safe to try right now; the few that change things are marked. You will finish with `sysinfo.zsh`, a one-screen summary of your Mac built from the same pipes you learned in [Pipes](#pipes) and the scripting structure from [Shell Scripting](#scripting).

Everything in the first four sections only looks. Run `ps`, `top`, `lsof`, `uname`, `sw_vers` and `sysctl` as often as you like. When a command can change state (`kill`, `defaults write`, `diskutil`, `launchctl bootout`, `softwareupdate -i`), read its card, run the read-only form first, and test on something you started yourself, such as a `sleep` process.
What a process is

A **process** is a running program: the kernel's record of its code, its memory, its open files and its identity. Each has a **process ID** (PID), a number the kernel assigns, and a **parent process ID** (PPID), the PID of the process that started it. The first process, **launchd**, has PID 1 and is the ancestor of everything else on macOS. Your Terminal window starts a shell, and the shell starts every command you type.

blocks.code:
launchd (PID 1)
     │
     ├── WindowServer, Dock, Finder ...        (system and login services)
     │
     └── Terminal.app  (PID 612)
            │
            └── -zsh   (PID 4242)              ◀ your shell
                   │
                   ├── ping -c 5 example.com   (PID 4310)   a child per command
                   └── sleep 600 &              (PID 4311)   a background child

blocks.text: A new process is made in two steps. The parent calls `fork`, which clones itself, and the child then calls `exec`, which replaces its code with the new program. That is why the shell can set up redirections between the two steps, as described in [Pipes](#pipes), and why a child cannot change its parent's variables or working directory.
A process is always in one **state**. `ps` shows it as a letter in the `STAT` column:

head: State
Meaning
Typical cause
rows: waiting for input, a timer or a network packet
stuck in a disk or driver call, cannot be killed until it returns
finished, but the parent has not collected its exit status yet

blocks.text: A **thread** is a unit of execution inside a process; a process has one or more, all sharing its memory. `top` and Activity Monitor show thread counts.

When a process ends it leaves an **exit status** that the parent collects with `wait`. A zombie is only a leftover record and costs no CPU. It disappears when the parent exits, so you cannot kill a zombie; you kill its parent.
Looking at processes: ps, top, pgrep, lsof
The BSD tools on macOS differ from Linux in flags and output. Learn the macOS spellings once.
The three commands above are the simplest "who am I running on" checks. The real tools of this section are below; the outputs shown are samples, and yours will list your own processes.

blocks.code:
$ ps -Ao pid,ppid,%cpu,%mem,etime,comm -r | head -4

 5120   612   3.1  0.8       12:03 /Applications/Utilities/Terminal.app/Contents/MacOS/Terminal

$ lsof -nP -iTCP -sTCP:LISTEN | awk 'NR > 1 {print $1, $2, $9}'
rapportd 612 *:49152
Python 51234 *:8000
ControlCe 701 *:7000

blocks.name: ps
blocks.sum: Print a snapshot of running processes, with columns you choose.

how.text: `ps` reads the kernel's process table once and prints it. With no options it shows only the processes on your current terminal. `ps aux` (BSD style, no dash) shows every process of every user with CPU and memory percentages, and `ps -A` or `ps -e` lists all processes with the default columns. `-o` picks exactly the columns you want, which is how you make the output easy to parse.

macOS `ps` can sort for you: `-r` orders by current CPU use and `-m` by memory. `-c` shows only the executable name instead of the full command line, which matters because paths on macOS contain spaces (`/Applications/Google Chrome.app/...`) and break whitespace-based parsing.

Useful keywords: `pid`, `ppid`, `user`, `%cpu`, `%mem`, `rss` (resident memory in KB), `vsz` (virtual size), `etime` (elapsed time since start), `lstart` (full start time), `state`, `comm` (executable), `command` (full command line).

flags.d: BSD style: all users (a), user-oriented columns (u), including processes with no terminal (x).
Choose and order the output columns; `-o pid=` removes a header.
Only these process IDs, comma separated.
Sort by CPU usage, highest first.
Sort by memory usage, highest first.
Show only the executable name in the command column.

gotchas: The `[s]shd` trick works because the regex `[s]shd` matches the text `sshd` but not the text `grep [s]shd` that is shown in the process list, so `grep` does not find itself. `pgrep` avoids the problem completely.
`ps -ef` works on macOS but the columns differ from Linux. Use `-o` for portable parsing. There is no `--sort` option: use `-r`, `-m` or `sort`.

blocks.name: top
blocks.sum: A live, continuously updated table of processes, CPU, memory and load.
blocks.syntax: top [-o key] [-O key] [-l samples] [-n nprocs] [-s seconds] [-stats keys] [-pid pid]

how.text: Run `top` on its own and it redraws every second until you press `q`. Press `o` then a key name such as `mem` to change the sort. For scripting, `-l N` turns it into **logging mode**: it prints N samples as plain text and exits. `-n` limits the number of processes shown and `-o` sets the sort key (`cpu`, `mem`, `pid`, `command`, `time`, `threads`, and others).

The CPU percentage of every process is computed as a change between two samples, so in logging mode the **first sample shows invalid CPU values**. Ask for two samples (`-l 2`) and use the second. `-stats pid,command,cpu,mem` limits the columns to exactly what you need.

flags.d: Sort by this key, descending. Prefix `+` for ascending.
Logging mode: print N samples and exit (0 means forever).
Show only the first N processes.
Comma-separated columns to show, for example `pid,command,cpu,mem`.

examples.desc: Interactive view sorted by memory
A parseable snapshot of the top five CPU users
Print only the second (valid) sample
Current CPU usage line (user, sys and idle percentages)

gotchas: `top -l 1` looks right but its CPU column is not valid, so scripts that use one sample see misleading numbers. Take the last of two.

blocks.name: htop
blocks.sum: An interactive process viewer with colours, a process tree, mouse support and kill built in.

how.text: Install it with `brew install htop`. It shows per-core CPU bars, memory and swap meters, and a sortable list. Function keys do the work: `F5` tree view, `F6` sort, `F9` kill (choose a signal), `F4` filter, `F10` quit. It reads the same process table as `ps`; it only presents it better. Some detail columns need `sudo` on macOS.

examples.desc: Watch your own processes

blocks.name: pgrep
blocks.sum: Find process IDs by name or command line, and (with pkill) send them signals.

how.text: `pgrep` matches a regular expression against process **names** and prints the PIDs, one per line. `-f` matches the full command line instead, `-x` requires the name to match exactly, `-l` also prints the name, `-n` and `-o` select the newest or oldest match. It never matches itself, unlike `ps | grep`. `pkill` takes the same selection options but sends a signal (default TERM) to every match.
The selection power is also the danger: `pkill python` ends *every* process with "python" in its name. Always run `pgrep -fl pattern` first and read the list.

flags.d: Match against the full command line, not just the process name.
Print the process name next to each PID.
Select only the newest matching process.
Select only the oldest matching process.

examples.desc: See what would match before you kill anything
Is the SSH daemon running?
examples.code: pgrep -x sshd > /dev/null && echo "sshd is running" || echo "sshd is not running"

examples.desc: Show CPU and memory for every process whose command contains a word
Safe kill by name: list, review, then act

gotchas: `pgrep -f` matches the shell that is running your command, because the pattern appears in its command line. If a script pipes `pgrep -f name` and gets one extra PID, that is the cause. Anchor the pattern (`pgrep -f '^sleep 600'`) or use `-x` with the name.

blocks.name: lsof
blocks.sum: List open files, and because everything is a file, also listening ports, connections and which process holds them.

how.text: A process's open files include regular files, directories, pipes, devices and **network sockets**. `lsof` walks the kernel's tables and prints one row per open file with the owning command, PID, user and the name. Without `sudo` it shows your own processes; with it, everything.

`-i` selects network files, so `lsof -i :8000` answers "what is using port 8000?" `-n` stops DNS lookups and `-P` stops port-name lookups (`8000` instead of `http-alt`), so output is fast and exact. Selections combine with OR by default; add `-a` to AND them. The port-focused flags are covered again in [Ports and sockets](#ports).

flags.d: Do not resolve port numbers to service names.
Only commands whose name starts with this.
With `-iTCP`: only sockets in the LISTEN state.
Everything open under a directory, recursively (slow).

examples.desc: Who is listening for TCP connections?
What process owns port 8000?
examples.out:
COMMAND   PID USER   FD   TYPE             DEVICE SIZE/OFF NODE NAME
Python  51234 sam    4u  IPv4 0x1a2b3c4d5e6f7081      0t0  TCP *:8000 (LISTEN)

examples.desc: What files does a process have open?

gotchas: `-t` prints bare PIDs and is made for `kill $(lsof -t -i :8000)`, but with no match it prints nothing and `kill` then complains about missing arguments. Check first.
Run as your own user, `lsof` hides other users' and system processes, so a port can look free when it is not. Use `sudo` to see everything.

blocks.text: Signals and stopping processes

A **signal** is a small message the kernel delivers to a process. Programs install handlers for some signals; the rest have a default action. The `kill` command is misnamed: it **sends a signal**, and most signals do not kill.

head: Signal
Number (macOS)
Default action
Typical use
rows: "terminal hung up"; many daemons reload configuration on it
cannot be caught or ignored; no cleanup runs
the polite default of `kill`; programs can clean up first
cannot be caught; resume with CONT
what [[Ctrl+Z]] sends; programs may handle it

blocks.text: Signal **numbers differ between macOS and Linux** (STOP is 17 here and 19 on Linux). Use names, never numbers, in scripts.
The escalation ladder for a process that will not quit:

items.text: `kill PID` (TERM). Wait a few seconds. Well-behaved programs save state and exit.
`kill -HUP PID` if it is a daemon that should reload, or `kill -INT PID`.
`kill -KILL PID` (also written `kill -9`) as the **last** resort. The process gets no chance to flush files, remove lock files or close connections, which can leave corrupted data and stale locks.

blocks.text: A PID is reused over time, and `pkill name` hits every match. Killing a system process (`WindowServer`, `launchd`, `kernel_task`) can log you out or crash the machine. Never run `sudo kill -9 -1` or `killall` with a broad pattern, and never kill a process you do not recognize without reading its command line first (`ps -p PID -o command`). Practice on a `sleep` you started yourself.

tokens.exp: no host-name or port-name lookups, so output is fast and numeric
only TCP network files on port 8000
only sockets in the LISTEN state

blocks.name: kill
blocks.sum: Send a signal to one or more processes by PID (TERM unless you choose another).

how.text: `kill PID` sends TERM, which asks the program to end. `kill -KILL PID` sends the uncatchable KILL. `kill -STOP` and `kill -CONT` pause and resume. A negative PID such as `-4242` targets a whole process group. You can only signal your own processes unless you use `sudo`. In zsh, `kill %1` takes a job number from `jobs`. `kill -l` lists signal names.

flags.d: The default signal: polite request to exit.

examples.desc: Start a sleeper, find it and stop it politely
Pause and resume
Send TERM to every process of a pattern, after a check
Does the process still exist after TERM? (signal 0 only tests)

gotchas: `kill -9` as a first move skips the program's cleanup. Use TERM and wait.
On macOS, `kill` cannot signal processes of other users or protected system processes even with `sudo`, if System Integrity Protection guards them.

blocks.name: killall
blocks.sum: Send a signal to every process with a given name.

how.text: On macOS `killall` takes a **process name** (not "kill all processes" as on some older Unixes) and signals every process of your user with exactly that name; with `sudo` it covers other users. It is the standard way to restart Finder, Dock or the DNS responder: `killall Dock`, `killall Finder`. `-v` prints each PID signalled, `-m` treats the name as a regular expression.

flags.d: Match the name as a regex.

examples.desc: Restart the Dock after changing a setting
Show which processes would be hit by a broad regex first

gotchas: `killall python3` stops every Python script you are running, including those in PyCharm. Check `pgrep -fl python3` first.

blocks.text: Jobs: processes owned by your shell

A **job** is a process or pipeline your shell started and tracks. A **foreground** job owns the terminal and reads your keyboard. A **background** job runs while you keep typing. The shell lets you move jobs between the two.

head: You type
Effect
rows: start the command in the background and print its job number and PID
stop (pause) the foreground job and return to the prompt
resume the stopped job in the background
bring job 1 (or job 2) back to the foreground
list this shell's jobs, with PIDs for `-l`
detach the job so the shell forgets it and will not send it HUP on exit
start a command that ignores the hangup signal, output to `nohup.out`
zsh shortcut: start in the background already disowned
pause the shell until background jobs finish

blocks.code:
$ sleep 600 &
[1] 4311
$ sleep 700 &
[2] 4312
$ jobs -l
[1]  - 4311 running    sleep 600
[2]  + 4312 running    sleep 700
$ kill %1
[1]  - terminated  sleep 600
$ jobs
[2]  + running    sleep 700
$ kill %2
[2]  + terminated  sleep 700

blocks.text: Press [[Ctrl+Z]] while a foreground command runs and zsh prints `suspended` and returns the prompt; `bg` then continues it in the background and `fg` brings it back. A stopped job has state `T` in `ps`.

Jobs belong to the shell that started them. If you close the terminal tab, zsh sends HUP to its running jobs (the `HUP` option is on by default), which ends them. For a long download or a server that must survive, either start it with `nohup`, disown it, or use `tmux`, covered in [SSH](#ssh).

blocks.name: jobs
blocks.sum: List the background and stopped jobs of the current shell; with fg, bg, disown and wait to manage them.

how.text: These are shell builtins that act on the shell's job table. `jobs -l` shows the PID as well as the job number. `%1`, `%+` (current) and `%-` (previous) name jobs, and `%?text` selects one by a word in its command. `bg` continues a stopped job in the background; `fg` returns it to the terminal. `disown` removes the job from the table. `wait` blocks until a job or PID exits and returns its exit status.

examples.desc: Run two things in parallel and wait for both
Start a background pipeline and keep its output in a file
examples.code: { awk '{print $1}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn > top.txt & } 2>/dev/null; wait; head -3 top.txt

gotchas: A background job that writes to the terminal still scribbles over your prompt. Redirect its output: `cmd > out.txt 2>&1 &`.

blocks.name: nohup
blocks.sum: Run a command that keeps going after you close the terminal.

how.text: `nohup` starts the command with the HUP signal ignored and, if stdout is a terminal, redirects its output to `nohup.out`. Use it with `&` for something that must survive your logout. For anything long-running and interactive, `tmux` is better because you can reattach to it.

examples.desc: Keep a slow ping log running after the window closes

blocks.text: Priority: nice and renice

Each process has a **nice value** from -20 to 20 (default 0). A higher value means "nicer to others", so the scheduler gives the process less CPU when the machine is busy. Lowering the value (raising priority) needs `sudo`.

blocks.name: nice
blocks.sum: Start a command with a lower priority; renice changes a running process.
blocks.syntax: nice -n increment command      renice -n increment -p pid

how.text: `nice -n 10 command` starts the command 10 steps nicer. `renice -n 5 -p PID` adds 5 to the nice value of a process that is already running. Use it for batch jobs such as compressing files or scanning a large tree that should not slow your work.

examples.desc: Compress something in the background without hogging the CPU
Lower the priority of a running process

blocks.text: Services: launchd and Homebrew
**launchd** (PID 1) is macOS's service manager. It starts daemons at boot, agents at login, and scheduled jobs. Definitions are property-list (`.plist`) files in these folders:
The [Shell Scripting](#scripting) chapter showed how to *load* your own job. Here is how to *inspect* what is running.

blocks.name: launchctl list
blocks.sum: Show loaded launchd jobs with their PID and last exit status, and inspect or unload one.
blocks.syntax: launchctl list      launchctl print gui/UID[/label]      launchctl bootout gui/UID/label

how.text: `launchctl list` prints three columns: the PID (a dash when the job is loaded but not running), the **last exit status** (0 is clean, negative numbers are signals) and the label. `launchctl print gui/$(id -u)/LABEL` shows the full definition, state and the program arguments. `launchctl print system` lists the system domain and needs `sudo`. `bootout` unloads a job; this stops it and, for a job in `~/Library/LaunchAgents`, it comes back at next login unless you also delete or disable the plist.

examples.desc: Which jobs failed on their last run?
Inspect one job
Count running vs idle jobs
examples.code: launchctl list | awk 'NR > 1 {if ($1 == "-") idle++; else run++} END {print run " running, " idle " idle"}'

examples.desc: Find a service by name

gotchas: Do not `bootout` Apple's own labels (`com.apple.*`) to "speed things up". Some are tied to login, networking or the display and take effect only after a reboot, and system ones are SIP-protected anyway.

blocks.name: brew
blocks.sum: Install, update, inspect and remove command-line tools and apps with Homebrew.

how.text: Homebrew keeps formulae (command-line tools) and casks (GUI apps) under `/opt/homebrew` on Apple Silicon. **`update` refreshes Homebrew's own index of what is available; `upgrade` installs newer versions of what you have.** Both are needed to get newer tools. Installing never needs `sudo`; Homebrew refuses to run as root.

`brew services` wraps launchd: `brew services start postgresql@16` writes a launchd plist and starts the service at login. `brew bundle` reads a `Brewfile` listing your packages and installs them all, a one-file recipe for rebuilding your toolshelf on a new Mac.

flags.d: Install a formula; `--cask name` for an app.
Refresh the formula index (small and quick).
Install newer versions of installed packages (use `brew outdated` first).
Show installed packages; `brew leaves` shows only those you asked for, not dependencies.
Version, dependencies and caveats of a package.
Find formulae and casks by name.
Remove old versions and caches; `-n` previews.
Install from, or dump to, a `Brewfile`: `brew bundle dump`.

examples.desc: Install the network tools used in this book
examples.code: brew install jq tree wget nmap mtr iperf3 httpie watch ripgrep fzf bat shellcheck tmux

gotchas: A "keg-only" formula is installed but not linked into `PATH`. `brew info name` prints the exact `export PATH=...` line in its caveats.
On Apple Silicon `brew` itself is at `/opt/homebrew/bin/brew`. If `command not found: brew`, add `eval "$(/opt/homebrew/bin/brew shellenv)"` to `~/.zprofile`.

blocks.text: Who and what is this Mac?

blocks.name: uname
blocks.sum: Print the kernel name, version and CPU architecture.

how.text: `uname -m` is `arm64` on Apple Silicon and `x86_64` on Intel (or inside a Rosetta shell, which is why it matters when Homebrew picks the wrong build). `uname -r` is the Darwin kernel version, such as `26.2.0` on macOS 27.2, not the macOS marketing version; use `sw_vers` for that. `-s` is the kernel name (`Darwin`), `-n` the host name.

examples.desc: Which architecture am I running as?
Choose a download by architecture
examples.code: case $(uname -m) in arm64) echo "apple silicon build";; x86_64) echo "intel build";; esac

blocks.name: sw_vers
blocks.sum: Print the macOS product name, version and build.

how.text: `sw_vers` reads the system version file. With no option it prints all three lines. With one option it prints just that value, ideal for scripts that need to branch on the OS version.

examples.desc: Show all three fields
Major version as a number for comparisons

blocks.name: sysctl
blocks.sum: Read (and, with sudo, change) kernel parameters: CPU, memory size, boot time, limits.

how.text: `sysctl` exposes a tree of kernel variables. `-n` prints only the value, which is what scripts need. Useful names: `hw.model` (the Mac model identifier), `machdep.cpu.brand_string` (the chip name), `hw.ncpu` (logical CPUs), `hw.memsize` (RAM in bytes), `hw.pagesize` (memory page size), `kern.boottime` (when the system started), `vm.swapusage` (swap), `vm.loadavg` (load averages). Writing a value with `sudo sysctl -w` changes the running kernel until the next reboot; do not do that unless a documented procedure tells you to.

flags.d: Print only the value, with no name.

examples.desc: Chip name and RAM in gigabytes
Find every variable about the CPU cache
Time since boot in seconds

gotchas: Variable names differ between Apple Silicon and Intel in places (for example `machdep.cpu.brand_string` exists on both, but many `hw.*` frequency values exist only on Intel). Test names with `sysctl -n name` before using them in a script.

blocks.name: system_profiler
blocks.sum: Print a detailed report of hardware, software, storage and network configuration.

how.text: This is the command-line version of System Information. Name a data type such as `SPHardwareDataType`, `SPSoftwareDataType`, `SPStorageDataType`, `SPNetworkDataType` or `SPAirPortDataType`, and it prints that section. `-listDataTypes` shows all of them. `-json` gives structured output you can feed to `jq`. A full report can take many seconds; ask for one type.

examples.desc: Model, chip, memory and serial number
Disks as JSON, then pick names and sizes
Just the chip and memory lines

gotchas: The report includes your serial number and hardware UUID. Do not paste it into forums unedited.

blocks.name: uptime
blocks.sum: Show how long the system has been up, how many users are logged in, and the 1, 5 and 15 minute load averages.

how.text: The **load average** counts processes that are running or waiting to run, averaged over one, five and fifteen minutes. On a machine with N logical CPUs, a load near N means fully busy, and much higher means work is queueing. Compare against `sysctl -n hw.ncpu`.

examples.desc: Read the load
Print load average as three numbers

blocks.name: w
blocks.sum: Show who is logged in and what they are running; who and last report sessions and history.

how.text: `w` lists logged-in sessions with idle time and the current command. `who` is the shorter list. `last` reads the login history, which is useful after a reboot or for checking SSH logins: `last -10` shows the ten most recent, `last reboot` shows system restarts.

examples.desc: Who is on this machine?
Count terminal (ttys) sessions in the recent login history; remote SSH logins also show a host name

blocks.name: cal
blocks.sum: Print a calendar for a month or a year.

how.text: `cal` prints the current month. `cal 10 2026` shows October 2026 and `cal -y` shows the whole year. For date arithmetic see `date` in [Shell Scripting](#scripting).

examples.desc: A given month

blocks.name: vm_stat
blocks.sum: Print virtual memory statistics, counted in pages.

how.text: `vm_stat` prints counters such as pages free, active, inactive, wired, compressed, and page-ins and page-outs. The first line states the page size: **16384 bytes on Apple Silicon**, 4096 on Intel. Multiply a count by the page size (`sysctl -n hw.pagesize`) to get bytes. macOS uses spare RAM as a cache, so "free" is small by design; what matters is memory pressure and swap use. `memory_pressure` prints a summary, and Activity Monitor graphs it.

examples.desc: First lines of the report
examples.out:
Mach Virtual Memory Statistics: (page size of 16384 bytes)
Pages free:                               54321.
Pages active:                            200000.
Pages inactive:                          190000.

examples.desc: Free plus speculative memory in megabytes
examples.code: vm_stat | awk -v pg=$(sysctl -n hw.pagesize) '/Pages (free|speculative)/ {gsub(/\./, "", $NF); f += $NF} END {printf "%d MB\n", f * pg / 1048576}'

examples.desc: A one-line memory pressure reading

gotchas: Values end in a period (`54321.`). `awk` treats `54321.` as the number 54321 when you add zero, and zsh arithmetic reads it as a float (so `$(( n / 2 ))` gives `27160.5`), while bash's `[[ $n -gt 5 ]]` stops with an error; strip the period first (`${n%.}`).

blocks.name: iostat
blocks.sum: Report disk throughput and CPU split over time.

how.text: `iostat -w 2 -c 3` prints a line every two seconds, three times, with KB per transfer, transfers per second and MB per second for each disk, plus user, system and idle CPU percentages. The first line is an average since boot; read the later lines for current activity. `-d` limits it to disk columns.

examples.desc: Three samples, two seconds apart

blocks.name: ulimit
blocks.sum: Show or set per-process resource limits, most often the number of open files.

how.text: Limits belong to a process and are inherited by its children. `ulimit -n` is the maximum number of open files, which is **256 by default for a macOS shell** and low enough to break a port scanner or a parallel download. `ulimit -n 4096` raises the soft limit for the current shell, up to the hard limit. `ulimit -a` lists them all.

flags.d: Soft limit (the one enforced; may be raised up to the hard limit).

examples.desc: Raise the limit before a big scan

blocks.text: Disks, images and backups

`diskutil list` and `diskutil info` only read. Verbs such as `eraseDisk`, `eraseVolume`, `partitionDisk`, `apfs deleteVolume` and `secureErase` destroy data immediately, and `diskN` identifiers change between boots. Never run them on a drive you cannot afford to lose, and check the identifier twice. For practice use a disk image (below), which cannot touch real disks.

blocks.name: diskutil
blocks.sum: List, inspect and manage disks, partitions and APFS volumes.

how.text: macOS disks have identifiers like `disk0` (a physical disk) and `disk3s5` (a slice or volume). Modern Macs use APFS, where several **volumes** share one container's free space; the one you use is mounted at `/System/Volumes/Data` and `/` is a read-only system snapshot. `diskutil list` shows all disks and their volumes, `diskutil info /` details one, and `diskutil apfs list` shows the container layout. `unmount` and `eject` are safe ways to release an external drive.

flags.d: Details for one disk or mount point.
Unmount and eject an external disk.

examples.desc: See every disk
Free space and file system type of the main volume
examples.code: diskutil info / | grep -E 'File System|Volume Free Space|Container Free Space'

examples.desc: List mounted external volumes

gotchas: Do not use `diskutil` to erase anything in this book. If you need practice, use `hdiutil` images.

blocks.name: hdiutil
blocks.sum: Create, mount and unmount disk images (.dmg), a safe sandbox for disk practice.
blocks.syntax: hdiutil create -size 50m -fs APFS -volname NAME file.dmg      hdiutil attach file.dmg      hdiutil detach /Volumes/NAME

how.text: A disk image is a file that acts as a disk. `hdiutil create` makes one with a file system inside, `attach` mounts it under `/Volumes`, and `detach` unmounts it. Because the "disk" is only a file, you can practise copying, filling, and unmounting without any risk to real storage. `hdiutil info` lists mounted images.

flags.d: Make a new image; use `-size`, `-fs` (file system, e.g. `APFS` or `HFS+`) and `-volname`.
Unmount it; use the mount point or the `diskN` it printed.

examples.desc: Make a 50 MB scratch disk, use it, and remove it
examples.code:
hdiutil create -size 50m -fs APFS -volname Scratch ~/scratch.dmg
hdiutil attach ~/scratch.dmg
cp {{file}} /Volumes/Scratch/ && ls -l /Volumes/Scratch
hdiutil detach /Volumes/Scratch

examples.desc: Show the file behind each attached image

blocks.name: mdutil
blocks.sum: Show or control Spotlight indexing for a volume.
blocks.syntax: mdutil -s [volume]      sudo mdutil -i on|off volume      sudo mdutil -E volume

how.text: `mdutil -s /` prints whether indexing is enabled. `-i off` disables it, and `-E` erases and rebuilds the index (slow, and Spotlight search is incomplete until it finishes). It matters here because `mdfind` and `mdls` from [Files](#files) depend on the index.

examples.desc: Is Spotlight on for the main volume?

blocks.name: tmutil
blocks.sum: Query and control Time Machine from the command line.
blocks.syntax: tmutil listbackups | latestbackup | destinationinfo | startbackup | listlocalsnapshots /

how.text: Read-only verbs tell you where backups go and which exist: `destinationinfo`, `latestbackup`, `listbackups`. `listlocalsnapshots /` shows APFS snapshots kept on the Mac itself. `startbackup` begins one now. Some verbs need `sudo`, and the terminal app needs Full Disk Access (see the protections section below).

examples.desc: When was the last backup?
Count local snapshots

blocks.text: Power, settings and updates

blocks.name: caffeinate
blocks.sum: Prevent the Mac from sleeping while a command runs or for a set time.

how.text: `caffeinate` creates a power assertion so macOS does not sleep. `-i` blocks idle sleep, `-d` keeps the display on, `-m` keeps the disk awake, `-s` blocks system sleep when on AC power, and `-u` declares user activity. `-t N` limits it to N seconds and `-w PID` holds until a process ends. Given a command, it holds only while that command runs, which makes it the right wrapper for long downloads, backups and scans.

flags.d: Hold until the process with this PID exits.

examples.desc: Keep awake for one hour
Keep awake only while a long command runs
See who is blocking sleep

blocks.name: pmset
blocks.sum: Show or change power-management settings; query battery and sleep assertions.
blocks.syntax: pmset -g [batt | assertions | log | live]      sudo pmset -a setting value

how.text: `pmset -g` prints the active settings, `pmset -g batt` the battery percentage and charging state, `pmset -g assertions` what is currently preventing sleep (which is where `caffeinate` shows up), and `pmset -g log` the sleep and wake history. Settings changes need `sudo` and persist; read before you write, and note the old value.

examples.desc: Battery level and state
examples.out:
Now drawing from 'Battery Power'
 -InternalBattery-0 (id=4653155)	87%; discharging; 5:12 remaining present: true

examples.desc: Just the percentage
Why did my Mac not sleep?

gotchas: A desktop Mac has no battery, so `pmset -g batt` prints only the power source. Scripts must handle the empty case.

blocks.name: defaults
blocks.sum: Read, write and delete application preferences stored in property lists.

how.text: Most macOS apps and the system keep settings as **property lists** under `~/Library/Preferences`, keyed by a **domain** such as `com.apple.dock` or the global `NSGlobalDomain` (also `-g`). `defaults read domain key` prints a value; `defaults write domain key -type value` sets it, with the type given explicitly (`-bool`, `-int`, `-string`, `-float`). Changes apply when the app next reads them, often after restarting it with `killall Dock`, `killall Finder` or `killall SystemUIServer`.
Read first, record the old value, then write. `defaults delete` returns a key to its default.

flags.d: Set a key; add the type flag.
Remove a key (back to the default).
List the domains that have preferences.
Print the domain as XML plist.

examples.desc: Is the system in dark mode? (The key exists only in dark mode)
Show file extensions in Finder, then restart Finder
examples.code: defaults write NSGlobalDomain AppleShowAllExtensions -bool true && killall Finder

examples.desc: Undo a change
examples.code: defaults delete NSGlobalDomain AppleShowAllExtensions && killall Finder

examples.desc: Find which domains mention a word

gotchas: Typing the wrong type writes the wrong thing: `-string true` is not `-bool true`. Always specify the type, and check with `defaults read-type domain key`.

Sandboxed apps keep preferences in `~/Library/Containers/<bundle id>/...`, so `defaults` on the plain domain may not change them. The `cfprefsd` daemon caches values; `killall cfprefsd` flushes it if a change seems ignored.

blocks.name: plutil
blocks.sum: Validate, print and convert property-list files.
blocks.syntax: plutil -p file | -lint file | -convert xml1|json|binary1 [-o out] file | -extract keypath raw file

how.text: `-p` prints any plist, binary or XML, in a readable form. `-lint` validates syntax and is the right check before loading a launchd job. `-convert json` turns a plist into JSON (so `jq` can read it) and `-convert xml1` makes the editable form. `-extract key raw -o - file` prints a single value for scripts.

flags.d: Check that the file is a valid plist.

examples.desc: Read the version of an app from its Info.plist
A plist as JSON, then a field

blocks.name: softwareupdate
blocks.sum: List and install macOS updates from the command line.

how.text: `softwareupdate -l` lists available updates and is safe. `--history` shows installed ones. `-i` installs a named update and `-i -a` installs all, which may reboot the Mac without further warning and needs `sudo`. Install from System Settings unless you are managing a machine remotely.

examples.desc: What updates are waiting?
Names of available updates only

gotchas: `softwareupdate -i -a` can restart the machine. Save your work first.

blocks.text: Logs

macOS keeps one **unified log** for the kernel, system services and apps. `log show` reads history and `log stream` follows it live. Output is enormous, so you always filter, usually with a **predicate**: a small expression over fields such as `process`, `subsystem` and `eventMessage`.

tokens.exp: read stored entries (log stream follows live)
keep entries whose process is sshd; quote it so the shell leaves the double quotes alone

blocks.name: log
blocks.sum: Read and stream the macOS unified log, filtered by process, subsystem or message text.

how.text: `log show --last 10m` prints the last ten minutes of **default-level** entries; `--info` and `--debug` add the more verbose levels. `--predicate` filters: `'process == "sshd"'`, `'subsystem == "com.apple.network"'`, `'eventMessage CONTAINS "error"'`; combine with `and` and `or`. `--style compact` shortens each line. `log stream` does the same live and runs until [[Ctrl+C]]. Without `sudo` you see only your own user's records; many system messages need `sudo`.

flags.d: Filter expression; single-quote it so the shell leaves it alone.

examples.desc: Recent sshd activity
Watch Wi-Fi events live
Count error lines per process in the last hour
examples.code: log show --last 1h --style compact --predicate 'eventMessage CONTAINS "error"' | awk '{print $4}' | sed 's/\[.*//' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head

gotchas: Always include `--last` (or `--start`) with `log show`. Without it the command tries to read the whole history and takes very long.

blocks.text: Talking to the desktop: osascript, say, screencapture, sips

blocks.name: osascript
blocks.sum: Run AppleScript or JavaScript for Automation to script apps and show dialogs and notifications.

how.text: AppleScript controls scriptable apps through Apple events. One `-e` argument is one line of script. It is the quickest way for a shell script to show a notification, open a dialog, or ask Finder or Music to do something. The first time a script controls another app macOS asks for **Automation** permission for the terminal.

examples.desc: Show a notification when a long command ends
examples.code: sleep 5; osascript -e 'display notification "build finished" with title "Terminal"'

examples.desc: Read the output volume
Notify with the result of a check
examples.code: netcheck.zsh -q && osascript -e 'display notification "network OK"' || osascript -e 'display notification "network problem"'

gotchas: Quotes nest: the AppleScript text is inside single quotes for the shell and double quotes for AppleScript. A `'` inside the script breaks the line.

blocks.name: say
blocks.sum: Speak text aloud, or write speech to an audio file.

how.text: `say` uses the system speech synthesizer. `say -v '?'` lists installed voices. `-r` sets words per minute, `-o` writes an AIFF file instead of playing. Appending `; say done` to a long command tells you when it ends.

examples.desc: Announce the end of a long job
Read a file's first line aloud

blocks.name: screencapture
blocks.sum: Take screenshots from the command line.

how.text: `screencapture file.png` captures the whole screen. `-x` suppresses the shutter sound, `-c` copies to the clipboard instead of a file, `-i` lets you select a region, `-T 5` waits five seconds first, and `-R` captures a rectangle. The terminal needs **Screen Recording** permission, or captures show only the desktop wallpaper.

examples.desc: Silent screenshot after a five-second delay
Screenshot, then report its pixel size

blocks.name: sips
blocks.sum: Inspect, resize, rotate and convert images.
blocks.syntax: sips [-g property] [-Z maxsize] [-s format jpeg] [-r degrees] in [--out out]

how.text: `sips` (scriptable image processing system) edits images in place unless you give `--out`. `-g pixelWidth` reads a property, `-Z 800` scales so the longest side is 800 pixels, `-s format jpeg` converts, `-r 90` rotates.

examples.desc: Make a copy that is 800 pixels wide at most
Print the dimensions of every PNG in a folder
examples.code: for f in ~/lab/*.png(N); do echo "$f $(sips -g pixelWidth -g pixelHeight $f | awk '/pixel/ {printf "%s ", $2}')"; done

gotchas: Without `--out`, `sips` overwrites the original. Always give `--out` while learning.

blocks.text: Protections: SIP, TCC and Full Disk Access
macOS adds several layers on top of Unix permissions, and they explain most "Operation not permitted" errors.

items.text: **System Integrity Protection (SIP)** keeps the system folders (`/System`, `/usr` except `/usr/local`, `/bin`, `/sbin`) read-only even for root, and protects Apple's launchd jobs and processes. Check it with `csrutil status`. Leave it on; the tools in this book never need it off.

**TCC (Transparency, Consent and Control)** gates access to Desktop, Documents, Downloads, Photos, the camera, the microphone, screen recording and automation. Permission is granted **per app**. When Terminal reads `~/Documents` for the first time you see a prompt. Manage grants in System Settings, Privacy & Security.

**Full Disk Access** is the broad TCC grant. Terminal needs it to read protected areas such as `~/Library/Mail` or the Time Machine metadata, and `cron` needs it to run jobs that touch protected folders.
**Gatekeeper and quarantine** mark downloads with the `com.apple.quarantine` attribute; see `xattr` in [Files](#files).

blocks.title: sudo does not bypass TCC or SIP

blocks.text: `sudo ls ~/Library/Mail` can still say `Operation not permitted`, because the block comes from TCC (the terminal app lacks permission) and not from file permissions. Grant Full Disk Access to your terminal in System Settings, quit and reopen it, and retry. SIP-protected paths stay read-only even then; that is intended.
Pipe recipes
The point of all these tools is that their output feeds something else. Four recipes you will reuse:
**Kill a process by name, safely.** Select, review, act:
If the first line prints something you did not expect, stop. The second line is the action, run only after you have read the list.
**Top memory hogs, with readable names.** `ps` reports resident memory in KB:

blocks.code: ps -Ao rss,comm | sort -nr | head -5 | awk '{kb = $1; $1 = ""; printf "%7.0f MB %s\n", kb / 1024, $0}'

blocks.text: **Watch one process.** Print its CPU and memory every two seconds until it ends:

blocks.code:
sleep 600 & pid=$!
while kill -0 $pid 2>/dev/null; do ps -p $pid -o pid,%cpu,%mem,etime=,state=; sleep 2; done

blocks.text: `kill -0` sends no signal; it only reports success if the process exists. Stop the demo with `kill $pid`.
**Disk and memory in one line.**

blocks.code: echo "disk: $(df -h /System/Volumes/Data | awk 'NR==2 {print $4 " free"}'), memory: $(memory_pressure | awk '/free percentage/ {print $5}') free"

blocks.text: `df` is covered in [Files](#files); on APFS the writable data volume is `/System/Volumes/Data`.
Common mistakes

head: Symptom
Cause
Fix
rows: the PID ended, or belongs to another user
stop the job with `launchctl bootout`, not `kill`
app caches the value or is sandboxed
TCC or SIP, not file permissions
grant Full Disk Access to the terminal
the pattern matched more than you thought

blocks.text: Practice

blocks.title: Start, find and stop a background process

task.text: Start `sleep 600` in the background. Find its PID in two different ways (the shell's `$!` variable and `pgrep`), confirm it is running with `ps -p`, then stop it politely and prove it is gone.

hints: `$!` holds the PID of the most recent background job.
`pgrep -fl 'sleep 600'` prints PID and command. `kill -0 PID` tests for existence.
blocks.solution:
sleep 600 &
echo $!
pgrep -fl 'sleep 600'
ps -p $! -o pid,etime,state,command
kill $!
sleep 1; kill -0 $! 2>/dev/null && echo "still running" || echo "gone"

why.text: `kill` sends TERM, which `sleep` obeys at once. `kill -0` sends nothing and just reports whether the process still exists. Practising on a process you started yourself is the safe way to learn signals.

blocks.title: Who holds the port

task.text: Start a web server with `python3 -m http.server 8000` in one Terminal tab. In a second tab, find the PID and command that listen on port 8000, then stop the server from the second tab.

hints: `lsof -t` prints only the PID, ready for `kill`.

why.text: Sockets are open files, so `lsof` can map a port back to a process. `-t` makes the output suitable for a command substitution. If two programs fight over one port, this is the diagnostic.

blocks.title: Stop and resume

task.text: Start `ping -c 100 127.0.0.1 > /tmp/p.txt &`. Pause it with a signal, check with `ps` that its state is `T`, wait five seconds, and resume it. Show that the output file kept growing only while it ran.

hints: The pause signal is STOP and the resume signal is CONT.
`ps -p PID -o state=` prints just the state letter.
blocks.solution:
ping -c 100 127.0.0.1 > /tmp/p.txt &
p=$!
kill -STOP $p; ps -p $p -o state=; wc -l < /tmp/p.txt
sleep 5; wc -l < /tmp/p.txt
kill -CONT $p; sleep 3; wc -l < /tmp/p.txt
kill $p

why.text: A stopped process keeps its memory but gets no CPU time, so the line count freezes. CONT resumes it exactly where it was. This is the mechanism behind Ctrl-Z and `fg`.

blocks.title: One-line status

task.text: Print a single line of the form `disk: 120Gi free, load: 1.52 1.60 1.58, procs: 412` using `df`, `sysctl` or `uptime`, and `ps`.

hints: `ps -A | wc -l` counts processes (including the header line, so subtract one).
blocks.solution: echo "disk: $(df -h /System/Volumes/Data | awk 'NR==2 {print $4}') free, load: $(sysctl -n vm.loadavg | awk '{print $2, $3, $4}'), procs: $(( $(ps -A | wc -l) - 1 ))"

why.text: Each `$( )` runs a small pipeline and returns a value that is spliced into the string. Subtracting one removes the header line that `ps` prints.

blocks.title: Break it on purpose: the self-matching grep

task.text: Run `sleep 321 &` and then `ps aux | grep 'sleep 321'`. Notice that two lines appear. Fix it three ways: with the bracket trick, with `pgrep`, and with `grep -v grep`. Then kill the sleeper.

hints: The extra line is the `grep` process itself, whose command line contains the pattern.
blocks.solution:
sleep 321 &
ps aux | grep 'sleep 321'
ps aux | grep '[s]leep 321'
pgrep -fl 'sleep 321'
ps aux | grep 'sleep 321' | grep -v grep
pkill -f 'sleep 321'

why.text: `grep` appears in the process list while it runs, and its own arguments match the pattern. `[s]leep` matches `sleep` but not the literal text `[s]leep`, so the grep process is excluded. `pgrep` never matches itself.

blocks.title: Inspect your environment

task.text: Without opening System Settings, report your macOS version and build, your chip, and how many gigabytes of RAM you have, each on its own labelled line.

hints: `sw_vers` and `sysctl -n` with the names from the cards.
blocks.solution:
echo "macOS: $(sw_vers -productVersion) ($(sw_vers -buildVersion))"
echo "chip:  $(sysctl -n machdep.cpu.brand_string)"
echo "ram:   $(( $(sysctl -n hw.memsize) / 1073741824 )) GB"

why.text: `sysctl -n` prints bare values and shell arithmetic converts bytes to gigabytes (2 to the power 30 is 1073741824).

questions.why: `kill` with no signal name sends TERM, which lets the program clean up. KILL is the last resort and cannot be caught.

questions.q: Why can `ps aux | grep sshd` list a line that is not the daemon?

options.text: The grep process's own command line contains the text it is searching for

questions.why: The grep process is itself in the process list and its arguments contain `sshd`. `grep '[s]shd'` or `pgrep` avoid it.

questions.q: Which command shows what is listening on TCP port 8000, without name lookups?
questions.why: `-i` selects network files, `-n -P` skip name resolution, and `-sTCP:LISTEN` shows only listening sockets.

questions.q: Why should you not trust the CPU column from `top -l 1`?

options.text: CPU use is computed between two samples, so the first sample is invalid

questions.why: `%CPU` is a rate. The first sample has nothing to compare with, so use `top -l 2` and read the second.

questions.q: Which signal can never be caught or ignored by a program?
questions.why: KILL (9) and STOP are handled by the kernel itself, so no handler can intercept them. That is why TERM comes first: it gives the program a chance to clean up.

questions.q: What does `ps -Aco pcpu,comm -r` do differently from `ps aux`?

options.text: It shows only the CPU percentage and executable name, sorted by CPU

questions.why: `-A` selects all processes, `-c` shortens the command to the executable name, `-o` picks the columns and `-r` sorts by current CPU use.

blocks.text: `sysinfo.zsh` prints your Mac's model, chip, OS, uptime, load, memory, disk, battery, network address and the three busiest processes, using only tools from this chapter. Each value comes from a small pipeline, which makes it a good place to practise `awk` and command substitution.
Step 1: Identity and uptime

`kern.boottime` prints the boot time as `{ sec = 1759500000, usec = 123456 } Sun Oct ...`. Splitting on spaces and commas makes field 4 the number of seconds since 1970, and shell arithmetic does the rest.

blocks.code:
#!/bin/zsh
# sysinfo.zsh - one-screen summary of this Mac
# Usage: sysinfo.zsh
setopt PIPE_FAIL NO_UNSET

row() { printf '%-10s %s\n' "$1" "$2" }

# --- identity -------------------------------------------------------------
model=$(sysctl -n hw.model)
chip=$(sysctl -n machdep.cpu.brand_string)
cores=$(sysctl -n hw.ncpu)
mem_gb=$(( $(sysctl -n hw.memsize) / 1073741824 ))
os="$(sw_vers -productName) $(sw_vers -productVersion) ($(sw_vers -buildVersion))"

# --- uptime from the boot timestamp ---------------------------------------
boot=$(sysctl -n kern.boottime | awk -F'[ ,]+' '{print $4}')
secs=$(( $(date +%s) - boot ))
up="$(( secs / 86400 ))d $(( secs % 86400 / 3600 ))h $(( secs % 3600 / 60 ))m"

blocks.text: Step 2: Memory, disk, load and battery

blocks.code:
pg=$(sysctl -n hw.pagesize)
free_mb=$(vm_stat | awk -v pg=$pg '/Pages (free|speculative)/ {gsub(/\./, "", $NF); f += $NF} END {printf "%d", f * pg / 1048576}')
swap=$(sysctl -n vm.swapusage | awk '{print $6}')
disk=$(df -h /System/Volumes/Data | awk 'NR == 2 {print $4 " free of " $2 " (" $5 " used)"}')
load=$(sysctl -n vm.loadavg | awk '{print $2, $3, $4}')
batt=$(pmset -g batt | grep -Eo '[0-9]+%; [a-z ]+' | head -1)

blocks.text: `vm_stat` counts pages, so multiply by `hw.pagesize` (16384 on Apple Silicon). The battery line is empty on a desktop Mac; the report below substitutes a default with `${batt:-no battery}`.
Step 3: Network and the report

blocks.code:
iface=$(route -n get default 2>/dev/null | awk '/interface:/ {print $2}')
ip=
[[ -n $iface ]] && ip=$(ipconfig getifaddr $iface 2>/dev/null)

echo "== $(hostname) =="
row "model"   "$model, $chip, $cores threads, ${mem_gb} GB"
row "os"      "$os"
row "uptime"  "$up"
row "load"    "$load"
row "memory"  "${free_mb} MB free, swap used ${swap:-n/a}"
row "disk"    "$disk"
row "battery" "${batt:-no battery}"
row "network" "${ip:-offline} on ${iface:-none}"
echo "-- busiest processes (CPU %) --"
ps -Aco pcpu,comm -r | awk 'NR > 1 && NR <= 4 {c = $1; $1 = ""; sub(/^ /, ""); printf "%6s%%  %s\n", c, $0}'

blocks.text: Append Steps 2 and 3 to the file from Step 1 in order, make it executable and run it:

blocks.code:
$ ./sysinfo.zsh
== macbook.local ==
model      Mac14,2, Apple M2, 8 threads, 16 GB
os         macOS 27.2 (26B123)
uptime     3d 4h 5m
load       1.52 1.60 1.58
memory     926 MB free, swap used 1126.25M
disk       120Gi free of 460Gi (73% used)
battery    87%; discharging
network    192.168.1.23 on en0
-- busiest processes (CPU %) --
  23.4%  Google Chrome Helper
   8.1%  WindowServer
   3.0%  Terminal

blocks.text: The "free" memory looks small because macOS keeps spare RAM in use as cache. The number that matters is memory pressure, which you can add as a ninth row with `memory_pressure | awk '/free percentage/ {print $5}'`.

Add a `-j` option that prints the same data as JSON using `jq -n --arg`. Add a row for the top memory user. Run `./sysinfo.zsh` from launchd every hour, appending to a log, and plot free disk space over a week in [Python](#py-start).
**Next:** [See Your Own Network](#net-local) reads the interfaces, addresses, routes and DNS settings of your Mac, and starts the networking part of the book.

terms.def: Process ID: the number the kernel gives each running process
Parent process ID: the PID of the process that started this one
A small message delivered to a process, such as TERM, HUP or KILL
A finished process whose parent has not yet collected its exit status
Average number of processes running or waiting to run over 1, 5 and 15 minutes
The macOS service manager and process number 1
System Integrity Protection: keeps system files read-only even for root
Transparency, Consent and Control: per-app permission prompts for protected data and devices
Apple File System: the default macOS file system, with volumes sharing one pool of space
Property list: the XML or binary format macOS uses for settings and launchd jobs
A number from -20 to 20 where higher means the process yields CPU to others
A filter expression for `log show`, such as process == "sshd"
